articles.title_zh: Stocks slide again as Treasury yields push higher, Oracle leads Nasdaq lower: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
With yields on Treasurys continuing to push higher, consumers are likely to see interest rates on their borrowing rise — including for car loans, experts say.
Across both short-term and long-term Treasurys, yields have climbed as stronger-than-expected economic data has fueled inflation concerns and expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further.
Last week, the central bank's rate-setting committee boosted its federal funds rate — the rate banks charge one another for overnight lending — by a quarter-point to a target range of 3.75% to 4.0%. That benchmark can impact the interest rates consumers face when borrowing money, as well as how much their savings can earn.
The yield on 30-year Treasury bonds reached 5.446% Thursday morning, a level not seen since 2004. The 10-year Treasury note yield — a benchmark for mortgage rates — jumped to 5.15%, which was last hit in 2006. The five-year Treasury yield was above 5% in mid-morning trading, which is the highest it's been since 2006.
"Many auto loan interest rates move with the five-year or 10-year Treasury note. When bond yields are on the rise, we typically see auto loan interest rates move up as well," said Patrick Manzi, chief economist for the National Automobile Dealers Association, a trade group that represents auto dealerships.
"Given the run-up in bond yields recently, we expect that auto loan rates will be increasing as well," Manzi said.
Financing costs have already been edging higher, with new-vehicle loan interest rates rising about 20 basis points over the past two months and used-car rates up about 10 basis points in that time, Jeremy Robb, chief economist for Cox Automotive, said in a Sept. 21 report .
"Those moves are unlikely to change the average payment substantially, but they may weigh more on consumer psychology and further discourage big-ticket purchases," Robb said.
Lenders generally consider a variety of factors when determining the interest rate charged for an auto loan, including your credit score and credit history, experts say. The higher your score, the better the rate you'll typically qualify for. The lower your number, the higher the interest rate you may face if you're approved for the loan.
The loan term and whether it's for a new or used car also influence the rate. Used cars generally come with higher interest rates.
In the second quarter of 2026, the average interest rate on a new car loan was 6.35% — which is lower than the 6.79% average recorded a year earlier — and the average loan length was 5.8 years, according to a report from Experian , a credit reporting company. For used car loans, the average rate was about 11.2% in the second quarter, down from 11.57% in the same period in 2025, with an average term of nearly 5.7 years.
While the average price of a new car is about $50,000 , according to auto-pricing company Kelley Blue Book, Experian's data shows that the average amount buyers financed for a new car was $43,610 in the second quarter, with a monthly payment of $765. The average amount financed for used-car buyers was $27,852, with an average monthly payment of $542.
Interest rates charged can vary widely, however. For instance, auto companies' financing arms may offer below-market rates as an incentive to buy their cars, although those deals are often tied to slower-selling vehicles or offered instead of a larger up-front discount, Manzi said.
Even a 1-percentage-point difference in an interest rate can make a notable difference in monthly payments and total interest paid.
For illustration: A rate of 6.35% on a $43,000 new-car loan over six years — 72 months — would result in a monthly payment of $720 and $8,823 in interest paid over the life of the loan, according to Bankrate's auto-loan calculator . At 7.35%, the monthly payment would be $740, and total interest paid would be $10,306. At 8.35%, the loan would come with a $761 monthly payment and $11,814 in total interest.
To get the best interest rate possible, car shoppers should take some proactive steps, said Joseph Yoon, consumer insights analyst for Edmunds, a car-shopping website.

articles.title_orig: FDA nominee contradicts Trump on safety of measles vaccine
articles.title_zh: FDA nominee contradicts Trump on safety of measles vaccine
articles.content_orig:
Dr Heidi Overton faces confirmation hearing weeks after standing behind Trump as he suggested shot could be ‘quite lethal’
Dr Heidi Overton, Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), has told senators the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “safe and effective”, weeks after standing behind the president as he suggested the shot could be “quite lethal” .
At a confirmation hearing on Thursday, Overton described the MMR vaccine as “safe and effective”, adding: “It is our best tool right now in the public health response to the measles outbreak.”
Asked whether any vaccine on the US market was unsafe, she said: “Every vaccine on the US market right now is safe and effective according to the FDA.”
Overton faced questions from Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana Republican and physician who chairs the Senate health committee, whose vote is seen as pivotal. He had called her role in Trump’s August vaccine executive order “almost disqualifying”.
The hearing comes as the US records its highest number of measles cases since 1991.
When Cassidy asked what Overton would do if the president asked her to break those assurances on vaccine safety, she replied: “I would give him my best advice, and I would follow the statutory requirements for the role of FDA commissioner regarding individual product determinations for safety and efficacy.”
When Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, asked whether she would have “the courage to stand up to” a president who he said “lies all of the time”, Overton did not answer directly. “I have worked for the president for a long time now, and earned his trust because I have been part of robust discussions to bring him the best advice,” she said.
In her opening statement, Overton framed her agenda around speeding up drug development to protect US leadership in biotechnology. “We can protect America’s global leadership in biotechnology, but we have to act fast,” she said, pledging to make the FDA “the agency of the possible, rather than the impossible”.
Overton, whose father leads a church in her home town of Gallup, New Mexico, has described Colossians 3:23 (“Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters”) as one of her life verses since childhood.
Susan Collins, the Maine Republican senator, challenged her over the FDA’s August authorization of flavored vapes and nicotine pouches, including blueberry, mango and cappuccino. Collins said nearly 90% of young e-cigarette users choose flavored products.
Overton said there was “100% agreement from this administration that we must protect kids”, but defended the decision as recommended by career staff because “so many adults are using flavors preferentially”. She added: “If that standard is not appropriate, we should work on statutes to fix that.”
If confirmed, Overton, 37, would be the youngest ever FDA commissioner. A surgeon by training, she is now deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy, and served as a White House fellow during Trump’s first term.
In a February 2023 issue brief for the conservative America First Policy Institute, where she was chief policy officer, she criticized federal policies that allowed abortion pills to be sent through the mail, writing that abortion “is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly”.
She would replace Marty Makary, who resigned in May, and take over an agency still recovering from 2025 layoffs that cut its workforce by nearly 20%.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia thwarts Houthi ballistic missiles, Yemen's Saudi-led coalition says
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia thwarts Houthi ballistic missiles, Yemen's Saudi-led coalition says
articles.content_orig:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have been firing on Saudi Arabia from Yemen.
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.
Delegations from the U.S. and Iran entered negotiations in June aimed at a war-ending deal based on a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries.
Those talks broke down as the U.S. and Iran continued to exchange strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint. Trump then said in August that the U.S. would launch a "crushing economic operation" to force Tehran into submission.
Thee United Arab Emirates on Thursday suspended flights by Iranian air carriers to and from the country until further notice, according to the state-run WAM news agency.
In a statement carried by WAM, the General Civil Aviation Authority said that "the decision was made in light of the US ban imposed on Iranian airlines from using airports in various countries around the world."
The authority said it will continue to update relevant authorities and the public on any developments until air traffic between the UAE and Iran returns to normal.
Saudi forces intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles on Thursday, a military spokesperson said, following safety alerts issued for five regions of the country.
Col. Turki Al-Malki, the spokesperson for Saudi-led coalition forces operating in support of the internationally-backed Yemeni government, said in posts to X that air defenses "thwarted an attempt to target Taif and Yanbu," two of the five regions put under safety alert.
"Escalations and violations by the terrorist Houthi militia will be dealt with firmly," he added.
The Saudi General Directorate of Civil Defence on Thursday issued safety alerts for five regions amid continued cross-border hostilities with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
The directorate posted safety alerts to X for the regions of Yanbu, Tabuk, Taif, Mecca and Jeddah.
All warnings were lifted soon after they were announced, with the directorate saying that the "danger has passed."
Senior Iranian figures praised Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's Wednesday address to the United Nations General Assembly, in which he said Tehran "will never bow" to U.S. threats.
Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, the chief of staff of the Iranian armed forces, wrote in a post on X that Pezeshkian's speech constituted "a slap in the face" to the U.S., after President Donald Trump said he was mulling a "big decision" at to whether to make a deal with Tehran or "quickly annihilate" the country.
"As long as Iran's waters, land and skies remain under threat, no aggressor nation -- nor any supporter of such aggressors -- shall enjoy security," Abdollahi said.
The speaker of the Iranian parliament and Tehran's chief negotiator, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, said in a post to X that Pezeshkian "spoke not just for a government, but for a 3,000-year-old civilization. He was the powerful voice of courage, resilience and strength for the Islamic Republic of Iran."

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled TPLF attacks in first comment on fresh Tigray fighting
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled TPLF attacks in first comment on fresh Tigray fighting
articles.content_orig:
Tigrayan fighters have been seen on the streets of the region's main city but it is relatively quiet there as clashes flare up elsewhere
Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks from Tigrayan forces and their allies in parts of the north of the country, in its first statement since fighting broke out on Wednesday.
The army said hostilities began in an area of Amhara region close to the border with Tigray, adding that its soldiers had inflicted heavy casualties and seized weapons.
The developments come as tensions between the federal government and Tigrayan leaders have sharply escalated over the last few days, raising fears that a devastating civil war could resume.
On Wednesday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominates the region, seized control of three airports from federal police.
The TPLF has not commented on the army's claims and the BBC has not been able to independently verify the army's claims.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.
There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara.
A humanitarian source in Afar told AFP news agency on Thursday that Tigrayan forces had launched heavy artillery attacks as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the border with Tigray.
"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice-president Amanuel Assefa is quoted by the news agency as saying.
The latest escalation follows months of rising tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and Tigray authorities, who fought a devastating war from 2020 to 2022.
That ended in an African Union-brokered peace deal but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating the agreement.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.
This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.
A Mekelle resident told the BBC's Newsday programme on Thursday there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere.
Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates
"Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash.
"People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash."
Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash".
With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC.

articles.title_orig: Dolly Parton's sister defends iconic singer's nephew over restraining order: 'We all love Bryan.'
articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton's sister defends iconic singer's nephew over restraining order: 'We all love Bryan.'
articles.content_orig:
By CHRISTINE RENDÓN, US SENIOR REPORTER and ADAM S. LEVY, US SENIOR SHOWBUSINESS REPORTER
Published: 12:33 EDT, 24 September 2026 | Updated: 12:37 EDT, 24 September 2026
The on-going feud between Dolly Parton's estate and her nephew continues to unfold.
Parton 's estate has reportedly been granted a temporary restraining order against the music legend's nephew Bryan Seaver following allegations he made threatening overtures towards her manager Danny Nozell.
Nozell, who managed Parton for over 20 years, took out a temporary restraining order against Seaver under Parton's company She’s Alive, LLC, and claimed Seaver demanded money from him and began 'invoking his self-proclaimed military-contractor experience, access to weapons, and capacity for violence' while doing so.
Seaver served as his aunt's security chief and was entrusted by her to announce the news of her death last month.
Now a Tennessee judge has granted Parton's company She’s Alive, LLC legal protection from Seaver and his security company Squadron Augmented Protection Services (SAPS), according to TMZ .
Seaver and SAPS must remain 1,000 feet away from She's Alive employees, lawyers, and business partners. Seaver and SAPS must also not interfere with She's Alive's business relationships.
Dolly Parton's estate has now been granted a restraining order against the music legend's nephew Bryan Seaver following allegations he made threatening overtures against her manager Danny Nozell; Seaver seen above with the singer in 2017 in NYC
Nozell, who managed Parton for over 20 years, took out a temporary restraining order against Seaver under Parton's company She’s Alive, LLC; Above, Parton and Nozell in LA in 2022
The issue will be addressed at a hearing scheduled for October 7.
The Daily Mail has contacted Nozell, Seaver's organization SAPS, and Nozell's attorney Timothy L Warnock for comment.
In documents seeking the temporary restraining order, Nozell told the court he fired Seaver from his position on September 15 as a result of the alleged threats, TMZ previously reported.
Nozell claimed that Seaver's behavior continued to escalate in the weeks ahead of Parton's August 25 death at 80, according to the outlet.
According to legal documents reviewed by TMZ, Seaver told Nozell: 'Her money better be bigger than I can make elsewhere or I'm going to f*** everyone. I am about to become the hand of retribution for my entire family.'
Another communication Seaver sent to Nozell, according to the filing, read: 'All I do is warfare … everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.'
Seaver allegedly told Nozell he was planning on setting 'up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnership and telling the violations these people have done on us,' per the court filing, TMZ reported.
Nozell requested that the court order Seaver to remain a minimum of 1,000 feet from Parton's office and to refrain from contacting Parton's businesses or affiliates, according to the report.
In response to the restraining order request, Seaver told TMZ on Tuesday: 'I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer.
'However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.'
The music legend died at age 80 last month, sending fans and the music world into mourning
Nozell said in documents previously viewed by TMZ that Seaver demanded money from him and invoked 'his self-proclaimed military-contractor experience, access to weapons, and capacity for violence' while doing so; Parton seen in 2023 in Nashville, Tennessee
Bryan said that the texts included in the filing had been published out of context to make it look like he was trying to be intimidating, which wasn't the case.
'I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster,' Bryan told the outlet. 'A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.'
Seaver said that one remark – in which he said he was going to 'rat f***' an organization whose name was redacted from the report – was 'about people that have done bad to Dolly in business.'
He added: 'Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that.'
Seaver last week received a notice reviewed by TMZ that he and his security organizations, which provided protection for Parton's Nashville home, museum and a warehouse, were being replaced by another company.
Insiders told the outlet that they believed Parton's manager Nozell and Pinnacle Bank were responsible for the decision to terminate him and his employees.
A new security team was deployed to the locations previously overseen by Seaver's companies after the termination notice was issued, according to the report.
Sources close to Seaver said that he and his associates had been 'dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions' carried out in the wake of Parton's passing.
Seaver seen accompanying Parton to a Jimmy Kimmel Live appearance in 2016
'We remain unshakably resolved to fulfill her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith,' Seaver's camp told TMZ.
They told the outlet that they believed the actions had been taken 'with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.'
According to TMZ, the notice issued to Seaver indicated that the DP Dean Trust had been overseeing Parton's business and properties in the wake of her passing.
Seaver retains a personal interest in her trust moving forward, according to the report.
Seaver, whose mother Cassie is Parton's sister, had been appointed by the late Jolene singer to reveal her death in a public statement.
Following Parton's August 25 passing after a cancer battle, Seaver had been seen in a clip in which he revealed the sad news.
Seaver served as his aunt's security chief and was entrusted by her to announce the news of her death last month
'Dolly has lived in the light, and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by [late husband] Carl, her parents, and countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens,' Seaver said in the emotional clip.
In the clip, Seaver noted that his father Larry had held the security position before him.
He said that he had been her security head for the past 'two decades,' and had been working for her over the past four decades.
'I first went on the road with Dolly as a kid, getting a taste of the road life in the early 1980s,' Seaver said. 'Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn't even know was possible.
'Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent. By her example, we believed that anything was possible.'
He added: 'She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history. My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you.'
Parton has been well-remembered in the weeks since her passing, during which she received an expansive tribute at the Primetime Emmy Awards last week, which featured Reba McEntire and Sally Field.
Nashville International Airport is set to be renamed in Parton's memory following a vote from the Metro Nashville Airport Authority Board of Commissioners weeks back.

articles.title_orig: Meta Debuts Dedicated ‘Charm’ Device for Using Muse AI
articles.title_zh: Meta Debuts Dedicated ‘Charm’ Device for Using Muse AI
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is continuing his metaverse while simultaneously pushing forward on AI agents.
At Meta Connect , the Facebook co-founder revealed on Wednesday the Meta VR Glasses, a smaller and slimmer device compared to the company's older Quest-branded family of VR headsets, and a handheld device called the Muse Charm that works with the company's recently released Muse AI personal agent . He revealed the products while speaking on stage at the annual Connect conference for developers.
Zuckerberg shared few details about what Muse Charm can do, only to say that people will be able to speak to the gadget to interact with their Meta AI agents "without having to unlock a phone or open an app." He didn't say how much it would cost, but said that Meta needs to "finalize laying out the components" and is "planning to have this ready to ship in time for the holidays in December."
"We've packed a lot of technology with this little guy," Zuckerberg said. "So, if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you."
The Meta VR Glasses are slimmer and lighter than the company's older Quest-branded VR headsets, but they are also more expensive, costing $1,299 when they go on sale in spring 2027. They represent Meta's first VR device since 2024, when the company debuted the $299 Quest 3S.
The Meta VR Glasses are powered by an external puck that houses a Qualcomm processor and battery, allowing it to function as a mini-computer that also helps reduce the glasses' overall weight and size. The glasses are able to display better visuals than the older Quest headset, and contain sensors that track users' eyes and hand movements, which reduces the need to use controllers to interact with the device.
"We have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion, high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time," Zuckerberg said.

articles.content_orig:
By LAURA FOX, ASSOCIATE SHOWBUSINESS EDITOR
Published: 10:50 EDT, 24 September 2026 | Updated: 12:07 EDT, 24 September 2026
Macklemore has announced a string of Free Palestine gigs, after being kicked off Ed Sheeran 's tour sparked a huge backlash.
The rapper was dropped as a support act from Ed's Loop tour over pro-Palestine comments he made at the singer's New Jersey shows earlier this month.
After Macklemore was dropped from performing at upcoming dates, all of Sheeran’s opening acts – Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe, as well as his backing band Beoga – announced they would be leaving the tour in solidarity with the rapper and Palestine .
Ed has since been accused of 'bowing to the mob' after he apologised to his fans for his handling of the row.
In a post on Instagram, Macklemore said that his 'schedule has freed up a bit' in the wake of being axed from the Loop tour.
The star then announced he would be performing concerts in Dublin, Paris and London, beginning on October 26, with proceeds 'benefitting organisations supporting the Palestinian people and movement'.
He wrote: 'If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years.

'There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now.
'It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore. People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community.
'To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it.
'What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage. When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.
'So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit.
'I’ve spent the last week reaching out to artists who have shown up and used their stages to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences.
'Artists who understand that our platforms mean very little if we’re only willing to use them when it’s safe.
'Because of how quickly all of this has come together, a lot of the conversations, schedules and details are still being worked out. But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done.

'So we’re going on tour. FREE PALESTINE TOUR. Dublin, Paris, London.
'Artist announcements coming soon, as well as US dates.

articles.title_zh: Some reporters denied White House access despite judge overturning Trump media ban
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Reporters whose White House access was revoked after President Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the grounds were allowed to enter the complex again Thursday, hours after a federal judge ordered senior Trump administration officials to restore their press credentials.
Footage from MS NOW and CNN showed their reporters regaining access to the White House and broadcasting from inside the gates hours after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued his order granting the outlets temporary relief. Politico also reported its reporter was allowed to reenter the grounds.
Journalists from all three outlets were initially denied entry earlier Thursday morning, which prompted their attorneys to ask the court for an "immediate" hearing. The lawyers said top White House officials had "repeatedly violated" Kelly's order by continuing to turn away journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico. They began getting back onto the complex around noon.
In a sworn declaration with the court that became public soon after the reporters began coming back in, director of White House press operations Micah Stopperich said his office was notified at 7:10 a.m. to restore access to reporters impacted by the ban and started that process 15 minutes later. Secret Service then indicated at 9:07 a.m. that the press badges for those journalists were reactivated, and the credentials that had been confiscated were delivered to White House Operations staff at 9:45 a.m.
The reporters' badges were then left at the designated White House entry gate for members of the press just before 10 a.m, and Secret Service said those press passes could be picked up "as soon as they were delivered," Stopperich said.
The standoff over the banned outlets coincided with Mr. Trump welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House for a state visit, complete with elaborate ceremonies that were not broadcast by major U.S. television networks. The outlets had suspended most coverage of White House events in solidarity with CNN, which is a part of the five-member collaborative television "pool" that documents the president's activities.
In his decision issued after midnight Thursday, Kelly granted a request from the three news outlets to immediately reinstate their access to the White House grounds while they challenge Mr. Trump's move to ban them from the complex because of their coverage of his administration.
Lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico have argued that the restriction violates the First Amendment and their right to due process.
In an eight-page ruling , Kelly said the three news outlets are likely to succeed in showing that their due process rights were likely violated, writing that the journalists were not given prior notice of the bans or an opportunity to challenge them. And he noted that some of the CNN, MS NOW and Politico stories that the White House cited as justification for the bans were "routine" and, in certain cases, months old.
Kelly also said he is "skeptical" of the Trump administration's claim that the bans were motivated by national security concerns.
"[Nothing] in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns," said the judge, who was nominated by Mr. Trump during his first term. "Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs' reporting."
Kelly's temporary restraining order will remain in place for 14 days while he weighs granting longer-lasting relief.
"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court's swift action," Theodore Boutrous, a lawyer for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, said in response to the decision.
The Justice Department is expected to swiftly appeal the decision. Mr. Trump said on Truth Social earlier this week his administration would turn to the appeals court if Kelly ruled in favor of the news outlets.
On Thursday morning, Mr. Trump criticized CNN and MS NOW, and alleged a recent report from MS NOW was "FAKE NEWS."
"The Dumocrats make up lie after lie," he wrote on Truth Social . "The new one is that I want Ford's Theater named after me. That's where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated. Who would want that? I don't! It is FAKE NEWS started by MSDNC AND CNN."
Mr. Trump announced Friday that "effective immediately," he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because of their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS." On Saturday morning, reporters from the three outlets who attempted to enter the White House complex were turned away and had their press credentials taken by the Secret Service.
The news organizations filed a lawsuit challenging Mr. Trump's ban on Monday. Lawyers for the journalists said the ban amounted to unconstitutional retaliation for their coverage of the president and violated the Constitution's Due Process Clause because their reporters did not receive notice that the president would deny them access because of reporting he dislikes or an opportunity to respond to the decision.
"The President's statements make clear he implemented the ban to coerce more favorable coverage of the administration from CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from reporting that the President might view as unfavorable," lawyers for the outlets wrote.
CBS News and dozens of other news organizations submitted a friend-of-the-court brief in support of the three outlets, arguing that the Trump administration's reasons for banning them "are transparently viewpoint discriminatory."
The Justice Department has defended the president's ban , arguing in a filing that the news organizations' reporting raises national security concerns. They also said journalists for the three outlets failed to act with "professionalism and decorum."
"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," government lawyers wrote in a filing.
They argued that the White House has "compelling reasons" for restricting the reporters' access to the White House, including enforcing "minimum standards" of professionalism for the press and protecting classified information.
The Justice Department also revealed that the White House Press Office sent letters to each of the news organizations Tuesday notifying them that the president decided to revoke their journalists' hard passes.
The letters claim that the news outlets have "exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."
The White House gave CNN, MS NOW and Politico a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to respond to its claims.
The letters appear designed to address the news outlets' claims that the ban deprived them of due process.
But Kelly wrote in his decision that one of the standards of conduct cited by the White House in justifying the bans "is so vague it hardly does the trick."
In response to the Justice Department's argument that the outlets' reporting endangered national security, the judge said that so far, administration officials "offer little to back up their asserted national security interest to justify revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes."
"[E]ven the justifications provided to Plaintiffs after this case was filed are ambiguous about the true purpose of the revocations: while Defendants' letters to Plaintiffs mention national security concerns, they purport to identify reporting that 'threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods,' leaving open the possibility that all the stories fall into the lat[t]er bucket, rather than the former," Kelly wrote.

While Mr. Trump and Xi meet at the White House, the first lady and Xi's wife, Peng Liyuan, toured the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art in D.C.
Waving both Chinese and American flags, children from a local Chinese school gave a choir performance for the first ladies.
When President Trump visited Beijing in May, he and Xi agreed to pursue what they called "constructive strategic stability" — political-speak indicating a commitment to improve the world's most important bilateral relationship despite deep mistrust, suspicion and intense competition.
Four months later as Xi visits the U.S., Chinese analysts see little reason to hope for any major breakthroughs, and they say the bilateral relationship, far from easing, appears as strained as ever.
"I think after all these years, Americans should understand pressure doesn't work," Zhao Hai, an expert in Sino-U.S. relations and vice president of the Chinese Institute of Hong Kong, told CBS News ahead of the leaders' summit in Washington. "It doesn't work on Xi. It doesn't work on China, and it doesn't work on the Chinese people."
Mr. Trump and Xi are now meeting in the Oval Office.
Speaking inside the White House's Grand Foyer, President Trump reminisced on the friendship he and Xi have had for years.
"Im delighted to welcome you to the beautiful White House," Mr. Trump said. "Such a great honor. In May, we had the great privilege of visiting you in Beijing, where you received our delegation with spectacular and very beautiful hospitality. Now, Melania and I are honored to host you in Washington as President Xi becomes the first ever Chinese leader to make a second formal state visit to America."
"From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people," Mr. Trump continued.
The U.S. president said he and Xi have made "tremendous strides" for their two countries, including on balancing trade and increasing market access for farmers. The president said the two leaders will discuss "pressing issues" about security, technology and AI or what he calls super intelligence.
Mr. Trump said "both China and the United States are great countries."
Speaking in the White House's Grand Foyer earlier Thursday, Xi said both nations are leading in artificial intelligence, and called for the "development of AI, always under human control."
Mr. Trump has been insistent that the U.S. must continue to rapidly develop AI to beat China.
Xi said "cooperation may not solve every problem" for the U.S. and China, but he said it's necessary. The Chinese president also said he hopes Chinese companies are treated fairly in the United States.
"We should coexist in peace," Xi said, through a translator. "As I have said many times, China and the United States, as two major countries, set to gain from cooperation and will both lose in competition. We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one, and should be kept within bounds."
After he called to avoid conflict, Xi announced that two pandas from China will soon head to Atlanta's zoo.
Currently, two zoos in the United States have pandas. The National Zoo and the San Diego Zoo both received pandas from China in 2024.
Mr. Trump, Xi and their wives entered the White House Rose Garden to a welcome from the U.S. Army Old Fife and Drum Corps.
Mr. Trump and Xi walked along the White House colonnade, lined with the portraits of U.S. presidents.
Another U.S. military band then performed the "Battle Hymn of the Republic" for the world leaders as Mr. Trump, Xi and their delegations looked on. Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles are among the Trump administration officials present.
The president's daughter, Ivanka Trump, who is not a government official, and her teenage daughter, Arabella, are present for the ceremony.
Mr. Trump then ushered Xi toward the Oval Office.
Mr. Trump, Xi Jinping and his wife Madam Peng entered the White House foyer as "Hail to the Chief" played.
Several White House offiicals were also in attendance: Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Vice President JD Vance and his wife, Usha Vance.
After journalists for CNN, Politico and MS Now were denied access to the White House Thursday morning — even though a federal judge has temporarily blocked the president's ban of their outlets — the television network pool is not covering the president's movements and remarks. That means that, as of 9:58 a.m., there won't be network coverage of Xi's arrival and visit.
Xi and his wife arrived at the White House shortly after 10 a.m., and were greeted by the Mr. Trump and first lady Melania Trump.
Mr. Trump, Xi and their spouses immediately entered the White House.
The first lady's office says the meal will begin with a toast of Schramsberg "Blanc De Noir," a nod to the "Toast to Peace" President Richard Nixon and Premier Zhou Enlai shared in Beijing in 1972. The menu as released by the White House is expected to be the following:
Yellow squash velouté Wild mushroom fricassée Crispy pancetta Scallion oil
Sesame crusted sea bass Braised baby bok choy Roasted garden eggplant Sauce verte

Ahead of Thursday morning's arrival ceremony, Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social about meeting Xi and his wife at the airport.
"I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit - Better than ever. Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL!" Mr. Trump wrote .
In a separate post , he showed a photo of him and Xi with a plane in the background with a logo saying "Only Trump" written over it.
Republican Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Tuesday that the red carpet shouldn't be rolled out for Xi. And he rattled off a long list of things that trouble him about China and the Chinese Communist Party.
"Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party," Wicker said on the Senate floor Tuesday.
Democrats, too, are urging Mr. Trump to think twice.
"What China is doing in Iran should be stopped," Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut told reporters Wednesday, referencing reports that Beijing has assisted Tehran. "The president should not be feting and praising Xi. He should be telling him, 'Knock it off!' ... I can't go into the details, but it certainly is significant enough and possibly increasing that the president should be drawing a line here."
President Trump posted on social media on Thursday morning that AI will be a "big topic of discussion" with Xi.
"A big day with President Xi of China," Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social . "Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!"
Thursday's meeting between Xi and Mr. Trump comes amid the arms race between the U.S. and China over AI development as many have called for international regulation. Mr. Trump has so far resisted calls for regulation , and told world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly earlier this week that "whoever wins AI, wins."
President Trump and first lady Melania Trump have planned an elaborate arrival ceremony at the White House for their Chinese counterpart, marking Xi's first visit in over a decade.

articles.title_zh: Rare September Nor’easter set to slam East Coast with heavy rain, damaging winds
articles.content_orig:
Millions across the Northeast are bracing for an intense, multi-day Nor’easter this weekend that is forecast to bring heavy rain and strong wind gusts to the East Coast.
Forecast models still disagree on the storm’s exact track, but one thing is clear: wherever it goes, it will hit the region hard. Forecasters have high confidence in a long-duration onshore wind event that could bring significant coastal flooding.
Coastal flood warnings and high wind watches are already in place along much of the East Coast, with more alerts likely to be issued throughout the day Thursday.
The highest rainfall totals — 2 to 3 inches or more — are most likely from Rhode Island to eastern Massachusetts.
Powerful winds, including gusts up to 50-60 mph, risk toppling power lines and trees. Small shifts in the storm’s track will determine where outages and downed trees are most likely to occur.
Coastal flooding is expected to run 1 to 3 feet above high tide, and a full moon Saturday night could intensify the tides and worsen the flooding. Waves along the coast are expected to reach 12 feet in Ocean City, New Jersey, and up to 22 feet in New England.
Moderate to major flooding is likely from North Carolina to Nantucket, Massachusetts, with southeastern Virginia — particularly the Virginia Beach-to-Norfolk area — at highest risk for major coastal inundation of 1 to 3 feet.
Meanwhile, a separate storm is already pummeling the Eastern Seaboard, generating high winds and rough surf.
In Massachusetts, residents were seen this week hauling their boats out of the bay, worried about high tides and flooding from the Nor’easter. One person told NBC News he’d been “prepping all week for both wind and water.”
One couple even changed their wedding plans because of the storm — they had been set to marry this weekend on a Massachusetts beach.
And the Boston Red Sox moved Sunday’s game — the season finale — up to Friday to avoid any weather-related delays or cancellations.
In New Jersey, crews cleared debris from storm drains and flood-prone areas as emergency management officials urged residents to prepare for the incoming storm. Monmouth County Sheriff Shaun Golden recommended charging devices and stocking up on batteries ahead of possible power outages.
Elsewhere in the country, days of heavy rain in the Southwest have triggered major flooding, sending muddy waters sweeping through the streets of New Mexico. The El Paso, Texas, fire department said it has responded to more than 50 storm-related calls.
Off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, Tropical Storm Nolo threatens heavy rain and flash flooding, with more than 30 inches of rain  possible in some areas. Extreme rainfall remains the storm’s biggest risk.
Nolo currently has sustained winds of 50 mph and is expected to strengthen into a hurricane by Thursday night — potentially reaching Category 3 strength. As of the latest update, the storm was about 285 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, moving north at 2 mph.
Nolo is not expected to make direct landfall in Hawaii, but it could come close enough to bring tropical-storm-force winds to the Big Island and Maui as early as Thursday night, with hurricane-force winds possible by Friday night.
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Sam Brock is an NBC News correspondent.
Kathryn Prociv is a senior meteorologist and producer for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks to close 250 stores: 'Difficult decision'
articles.title_zh: Starbucks to close 250 stores: 'Difficult decision'
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Thursday announced it will close about 1% of its North American cafes as part of its turnaround.
Under CEO Brian Niccol, Starbucks has staged a revamp of its U.S. business that has focused on improving the customer experience, including in-person interactions at its cafes. The announcement marks the second round of closures in North America during Niccol's two-year tenure.
Starbucks expects to shutter about 250 underperforming cafes out of its more than 18,000 locations in North America. It was not immediately clear where the closing locations are.
"We have carefully reviewed our North America coffeehouse portfolio and identified locations where we do not believe we can consistently deliver the experience we want for customers and partners or where we don't see a path to acceptable financial performance," Mike Grams, Starbucks chief operating officer, wrote in a letter addressed to employees.
For fiscal 2026, Starbucks is now projecting net new openings of 440 cafes, down from its prior outlook of 600 to 650 locations. Those new cafes will come from its international markets.
"The Company continues to see significant longer-term growth opportunity ahead in North America and is actively developing a strong pipeline of new coffeehouses," Starbucks said in a regulatory filing .
Most of the closures will occur before the end of fiscal 2026, according to the filing. Starbucks' fiscal year ends later this month.
The company expects to incur about $300 million in restructuring charges related to the closures. About $200 million of that charge will be related to the costs of exiting leases early and paying employees separation benefits. The remaining $100 million will be noncash charges from the disposal and impairment of its company-owned restaurant assets.

articles.title_orig: Fury vs Joshua: Cardiff to host heavyweight fight on 11 December
articles.title_zh: Fury vs Joshua: Cardiff to host heavyweight fight on 11 December
articles.content_orig:
Tyson Fury will face Anthony Joshua in an all-British heavyweight showdown in Cardiff on December 11.
The long-awaited clash had initially been linked with venues in New York and London before promoters settled on the Principality Stadium in the Welsh capital.
After months of negotiations that threatened to scupper the fight, as Fury called for a rematch with Oleksandr Usyk , Saudi Arabian boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh announced the venue and date for the bout on Thursday.
“For 15 years no one has been able to make this fight,” he wrote on social media.
“Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over…”
Choosing the 80,000-capacity stadium in Cardiff, which has hosted the Champions League and FA Cup finals, as well as Wales national team matches in football and rugby, allows both fighters to finally start their preparations for the eagerly anticipated clash.
The fight, one of the biggest in British boxing history, will be broadcast on streaming service Netflix.
Fury, 37, defeated 46-year-old Mariusz Wach in Thailand in his most recent bout in July.
Joshua, 36, survived a pair of first-round knockdowns to beat the unheralded Kristian Prenga in his last fight two months ago.

Investigations are underway into the deaths of two University of Mississippi students after packages of kratom , from a retail store, were found at both scenes.
The students have yet to be identified. One body was found Tuesday in a campus dorm room and the other individual was discovered at their home off-campus, according to WDSU .
Kratom is a plant-based psychoactive drug, also known as "thang” or “ketum.” It is often sold at gas stations or convenience stores and is used as an alternative to pain pills or for opioid withdrawal .
More than five million Americans have used kratom, according to University of Michigan research. In some cases, the substance has proven to be deadly when combined with alcohol or other drugs.
In Mississippi, narcotics investigators had yet to confirm a connection between the two deaths but urged the public to avoid using kratom.
The drug comes from a herbal extract made from the leaves of a Southeast Asian tree, known commonly as Kratom. The extract been used in traditional medicine for centuries to fight fatigue and comes in powder, liquid and pill form.
Some products have greater potency than others due to being made with a compound found naturally in kratom leaves called "7-OH." Companies extract 7-OH and chemically alter the compound to increase the product's strength. These are the most dangerous forms of kratom, Yale Medicine says.
The drug acts as a stimulant in low doses but has sedative effects in high doses, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration .
It starts to work in just minutes, the Mayo Clinic stated. Effects can last a few hours, depending on dosage. Kratom is often used to self-medicate for pain, coughing, diarrhea, anxiety and depression but also opioid withdrawal.
Kratom can lead to psychotic symptoms and is addictive. The drug has not been shown to be safe or to have the ability to treat any medical conditions.
Common side effects include weight loss, dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, liver damage, muscle pain, constipation and high blood pressure. Taking kratom can also sometimes cause dizziness, drowsiness, hallucinations, trouble breathing and seizures.
Nearly all deaths from kratom involve other drugs or harmful substances, the Mayo Clinic states. There are a couple of hundred kratom-related deaths in the U.S. each year.
There have been several high-profile deaths connected to kratom use, including Memphis Grizzlies basketball player Brandon Clarke and Tyler Wall , a trainer for YouTube star MrBeast.
Kratom is typically sold online but can also be bought at some gas stations or smoke shops .
There are no government-approved kratom products, or legal over-the-counter drugs containing kratom in the U.S., the Food and Drug Administration says.
Several states have made it illegal to sell, possess or distribute kratom, according to Yale Medicine .
Kratom is banned in Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Louisiana, Tennessee, Vermont and Wisconsin.
More states have proposed bans, including California, New Mexico, Minnesota and Kentucky.

articles.title_orig: Jeff Probst Made ‘Survivor’ His Life’s Work. He’s Not Done Yet.
articles.title_zh: Jeff Probst Made ‘Survivor’ His Life’s Work. He’s Not Done Yet.
articles.content_orig:
Aaliyah Puglia may have been the first person voted out of Survivor 51 , but she hopes that is not her legacy.
"I want to redefine the first boot narrative," the Rhode Island chef tells Gold Derby the morning after her elimination in the season premiere . "You're working on so much limited information as far as what you know about people, and it's no indication of who you are or how you might've played had you gotten past that vote."
'Big Brother 28': How to bang your teapot for America's Favorite Houseguest
'Survivor 51' premiere recap: 'The Open Era' kicks off with the 'permanent uncertainty' of all 21 newbies marooned on 1 beach
Aaliyah also reveals an interaction with Jeff Probst that didn't make the final cut. After her Toka tribe lost the immunity challenge, she told the host that the banner reading "Sorry for you" felt "so harsh" and that others had that "same reaction." Despite the moment that rubbed salt in the wound, she's all smiles today as she proclaims, "We love sassy Jeff."
Also in our exit interview, Aaliyah explains why she wants Devin Way and Angelica "Jelly" Loblack to win Season 51, whether she could have chopped down the tree that caused Lewis Kelly so much trouble at Exile Island, and how her name "was hot" well before Tribal Council began.
Gold Derby: Unfortunately, you were the first person voted out of the show. How do you feel about that term "first boot"?
Aaliyah Puglia : I want to redefine the first boot narrative. So often it seems like one of the worst things that can happen to you on Survivor , and it's just not true. There are so many factors going into a first boot. You're working on so much limited information as far as what you know about people, and it's no indication of who you are or how you might've played had you gotten past that vote. Anyone who's played before, or whoever is out first on 52 or in future seasons, it is OK. Just own it, and be proud. Oftentimes, you feel like you want to hide. During pre-game, I didn't even want to promote the show, in a way. I was like, I feel so [disappointed]. But I'm just like, F that! I went out there, I applied, they chose me for a reason, and I did what I could do, and I failed. And that's freaking OK. People fail every day. I just happened to fail on CBS public television and everyone saw it.
I don't like the word "fail" either, because you beat out thousands of people.
Quote-unquote "fail," because in the Survivor world, they love to say, "That just has to be the worst thing is being out first." And it's just not. The worst thing is not being able to play at all.
What made you a Survivor fan in the first place?
For me, I was just so captivated by the fact that anyone can do this. They don't cast celebrities or all these special people. They cast regular people you can run into at the grocery store. There was a point where I just got tired of watching it. Like, F this, it's time for me to apply! I'm tired of being a viewer. I want to play now. I just love this game. All those things I said in the pregame about being flexible and adaptable and building relationships, you kind of saw that. I had two very strong people fighting for me on Day 3. I was like, "I'm going to run it up. I'm going to make it to the end." Obviously it didn't work out that way, but that's the way it was supposed to go, I guess.
The opening of your season mirrored Season 1 from 26 years ago. What went through your mind when Jeff started walking through the boat and you're throwing things over the edge and jumping in the water?
Jeff is incredible. The charisma on screen, you see it, but in person, you're just enamored. You're just like, "Wow, I'm here. This is it." And you just freaking go and you get after it. How I was untying the ropes on the first boat is why I put myself in that position in the challenge. I felt like I was really fast untying them, so I felt like I would be good in this section of the challenge for us. Inadvertently, it didn't work out that way. But it was incredible jumping off that boat and you're in Fiji and it's go time.
I want to get your thoughts on Lewis going to Exile Island and failing to chop down the tree. Could you have chopped down that tree?
Probably. It's so crazy because when I was watching it last night, somebody said, "Why didn't he go from the other side?" [ Laughs .] I'm like, "Wait, he actually should have gone from the other side." Look, I don't know how much better I could have done, truly. How much respect I have for Lewis after seeing that scene. The fight, and you're out there. Incredible, right? He tried his absolute best.
Aaliyah Puglia, Angelica "Jelly" Loblack, Jenna Doore, and Mike Pinsky in 'Survivor 51'
At Tribal Council, I got the feeling that you thought you were pretty safe until Patt [Cannaday] mentioned your name. Did that catch you off guard, or did you see that coming?
I knew my name was hot before Tribal, but definitely caught me off guard that she openly said it. I was like, "OK, Patt. All right, girl." I was very nervous going into Tribal. Ultimately, I just couldn't save myself. I tried and I fought during live Tribal and tried to switch the tides my way, but it was left up to my Shot in the Dark. By the time your game is left up to your Shot in the Dark, it's like, "OK, is God going to keep me or am I going to go to Ponderosa?" And I went to Pondi.
At what point did you know you were playing it?
After the dust settled and we have to sit back down after live Tribal, everyone came up to me and told me they were voting for me and Maggie [Nestor] told me to play it. So, for me, I mean, I was going to play it. I was probably going to play it had not tribal gone live, honestly. I felt that nervous.
By playing it, you don't get a vote. I'm guessing you would've voted for Jenna [Doore]?
For sure. And obviously, had I felt that my vote would've mattered or made the difference, I would've rolled the dice on it and I just would've cast the vote. But at that time, I was too unsure and I just didn't think my vote would've made a difference.
Who do you wish you could have worked with on the other tribe?
All of the helicopter alliance [Sharonda Cox, Ori Jean-Charles, Jelly, and Devin]. If it was just us, we would've been good. But also, I really got good vibes from Ana [Sani] initially. Alexis [Levine] I also really loved. I would say those two were standouts outside of the helicopter.
There is a new element to the immunity challenge. It looks like when the losing tribe is determined to be the loser, a banner comes up and says, "Sorry for you."
They did not show this [on TV], but I look up and I'm like, "Damn! That just feels so harsh." And Jeff's like, "Wait, Aaliyah, you didn't realize that at first?" I'm like, "No, I did not realize that the sign said that." [ Laughs .] I'm seeing everybody in the clip and I'm like, "I had the same reaction." It's like, "Oh, wow, we didn't have to do all that, but it's fine."
It's like rubbing salt in the wound.
Yeah! But we love "sassy Jeff" though. We love that.
The theme of this season is whales, and there's a huge whale skeleton at Tribal. What was it like walking in there and seeing the whole Tribal set?
Tribal is so incredible and Survivor is unlike any other, and they are the best at what they do. How you see Tribal on screen is how it feels. It feels so real, and you're talking to Jeff, and you're in that moment. Obviously, people are filming it, but you see nothing but that moment. Just walking in, you feel, "I'm here." You dream of Tribal, right? Not on the first day, not at my expense, but you can't help but be grateful to be there in that moment.
Real talk: who annoyed you the most on your tribe? Who were you so happy that you didn't have to see anymore?
To be honest, I have a high tolerance for annoyance, truly. To me, it takes a lot to really get under my skin. At that point, after three days, no one was really doing anything to me where I'm like, "I'm tired of you," genuinely.

articles.title_orig: What we know after officials say ICE detained a US citizen and left him injured in Chicago suburb
articles.title_zh: What we know after officials say ICE detained a US citizen and left him injured in Chicago suburb
articles.content_orig:
Days after local police said Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents detained a US citizen in Evanston, Illinois, and left him injured on the ground, questions are swirling about what happened during the targeted enforcement operation gone awry — and the circumstances under which federal immigration officers can detain people.
The Evanston Police Department said the man, whom police have identified only as an Evanston resident, resembled someone federal agents were seeking. The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement the man “was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself.”
The man was later released, local police said, after agents determined he was not the person they were looking for and learned he was a US citizen.
At the time of Sunday’s incident, five federal agents were operating in separate vehicles as they searched the area for their target, one agent told an Evanston officer.
The incident is the latest instance of a US citizen caught up in the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown, which has featured highly visible enforcement operations and aggressive tactics that have prompted nationwide protests, legal battles and political backlash.
Here’s what we know so far about the incident .
Around 9:49 a.m. on September 20, Evanston officers were called to the area after receiving reports of two men arguing, police said in a statement. When officers arrived, they found the man on the ground with several bystanders helping him, police said.
Officials called an ambulance after the man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth. Witnesses told officers they believed ICE agents were attempting to detain him, according to police.
While responding to the scene in Evanston, a suburb of Chicago, one officer encountered two SUVs near an intersection and spoke with an individual in one of the vehicles, who identified himself as a federal agent conducting a “fugitive investigation,” police said. The person was dressed in plain clothes and wearing a vest marked “POLICE” with federal law enforcement markings, according to police.
A DHS spokesperson told CNN, “ICE encountered an individual who resembled the target. ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement,” but said the man did not identify himself.
The ICE agents “later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself,” the statement continued.
Evanston police said they are continuing to investigate the incident, and officers are preserving available body camera footage and interviewing witnesses.
Evanston’s police chief met with the man at a local hospital, and an evidence technician photographed and documented his injuries. Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss said in a statement on X that the wrongfully detained man was treated for minor injuries at Saint Francis Hospital.
DHS said the man refused assistance from ICE agents — but did not address the man’s injuries in its statement.
Evanston police said its officer reported seeing blood on hands of the agent in the SUV, which the federal official said resulted from an injury he received while trying to detain the man. The agent declined medical treatment.
No further information is known about the man who officials say was mistakenly detained or the agents involved.
Surveillance video obtained by CNN provides another perspective of the encounter, which appears to show two agents and the man in an upright struggle before federal officials take him to the ground.
As the confrontation draws the attention of several people nearby, at least three drivers pull into the nearby parking lot and exit their vehicles, joining other bystanders, some recording.
Cellphone video recorded by a witness, which begins as the confrontation is already underway, shows the man being held on the ground.
Two agents are seen standing behind a black SUV, with one appearing to hold the man down, in the video obtained by CNN.
A man’s voice is heard saying, “I’m a f**king US citizen.” The officers, one of whom was masked and wore a hood, then appear to release him and step away from the man.
The man can be heard telling the officers not to touch him as they move away from him.
Moments after releasing the man, the two agents return to their vehicles and leave the scene, while the man continues to lie face down on the ground in the street. A man wearing a cap kneels beside the man, gently placing a hand on his back and appearing to call for help. Several other people can also be heard trying to assist him.
One witness, Miguel Olivares, told CNN affiliate WLS he was taking a break while helping out at a nearby Mexican restaurant when he noticed vehicles parked outside and a confrontation unfolding.
“It looked like police vehicles until I started hearing, ‘I’m a US citizen. I’m a US citizen,’” Olivares said, at which point he began filming.
“They were being rough with him; they had him pinned against the floor, and it looked like one of the agents hit him in the face,” Olivares said. He and others tried to comfort the man after agents released him.
In response to a CNN request for comment, a DHS spokesperson said, “ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use ‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.”
Kate Huddleston, a senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union Immigrants’ Rights Project, told CNN that under the statute, ICE has limited authority to make civil immigration arrests — with two qualifications.
Agents must first have probable cause to both believe a person is undocumented and the person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained, she said.
Huddleston explained that, for agents to have probable cause to believe a person is likely to escape, they must have reason to believe the individual could not be found in the future, which could include having few ties to the community, no family members in the area or no permanent place of employment where the person could be located.
“For a person who’s merely walking down the street or driving in a car, whom ICE happens to see, there’s not necessarily anything about an individual whom they encounter in the community that would give rise to reasonable suspicion, absent someone affirmatively stating something like ‘I’m undocumented,’ or ICE having some sort of evidence that that individual is undocumented,” she said.
Huddleston added that a person who is detained in violation of the Constitution can seek relief, including under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows individuals who have been injured by the “wrongful or negligent act” of a federal employee to file a claim for reimbursement.
DHS said its “enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence.”
“We know who we are targeting ahead of time,” the agency said. “If and when we do encounter individuals subject to arrest, our law enforcement is trained to ask a series of well-determined questions to determine status and removability.”

articles.content_orig:
Peyton Manning is expected to be on hand for Tennessee's SEC opener against Texas on Sept. 26 at Neyland Stadium, one of the marquee matchups of the Week 4 college football slate.
But the Vols legend will have more than just his alma mater to watch.
Manning will also see his nephew, Texas quarterback Arch Manning , play up close as he makes his first appearance at Neyland Stadium. Not only will it be the Longhorn quarterback's first start in one of the SEC's toughest road environments, but it will also mark his first trip to Rocky Top — believe it or not.
"I'm definitely excited to play in a hostile environment, SEC road game," the Longhorns signal-caller said earlier this week. "That's what it's all about."
Through Texas' first three games of the season. The highlight thus far for Manning has been the comeback he orchestrated in Week 2 against Ohio State at home, when he led the Longhorns on three scoring drives in the fourth quarter to erase a 20-3 halftime deficit.
"Smart. Got really good command and control of what's going on," Heupel said of Manning this week.
And so, with Texas making its first trip to Neyland on Saturday, curiosity has risen about whether Tennessee and Heupel were in on Manning during his recruiting.
Though his uncle is Tennessee royalty and he held a scholarship offer from the Vols , Manning ultimately focused his recruitment elsewhere within the SEC.
As USA TODAY Sports' Blake Toppmeyer noted in 2022, the SEC programs that were consistently primary contenders for Manning, the No. 1 overall prospect in the 2023 recruiting class according to the 247Sports Composite ranking, included Alabama, Georgia, Texas and Mississippi.
Like Tennessee, Ole Miss also had strong family ties working in its favor. Manning's grandfather, Archie Manning, and uncle, Eli Manning, both starred in Oxford and remain among the most accomplished quarterbacks in Rebels history.
Manning committed to Texas in June of 2022. He chose the Longhorns over the likes of Alabama and Georgia, though it was believed to be a two-horse race between the Bulldogs and the Longhorns.
"Committed to the University of Texas," Manning said in a social media post.
But because Manning did not really consider Tennessee, Heupel and the Vols centered their attention on Nico Iamaleava, the No. 2-ranked quarterback and No. 3 overall prospect in the 2023 recruiting class. Iamaleava, in fact, committed to the Vols before Manning committed to the Longhorns.
Iamaleava, of course, would last just two seasons at Tennessee before his ugly split with the Vols that was centered around an NIL dispute.
Yes, Manning did receive a scholarship offer from Tennessee during his recruiting process. As noted by the Knoxville News Sentinel, part of the USA TODAY Network, Manning did not make an official visit to Tennessee during his recruitment.

articles.title_orig: New Details Emerge About ICE Officer Who Shot Man in Austin
articles.title_zh: New Details Emerge About ICE Officer Who Shot Man in Austin
articles.content_orig:
AUSTIN, Texas — A Democratic congressman said Wednesday that a Venezuelan man shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas and then taken to a detention center has been told by a specialist he needs surgery to remove the bullet still lodged near his spine.
U.S. Rep. Greg Casar visited a federal detention center in south Texas where Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, was taken into custody after being shot Sunday in Austin by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.
Casar said Garces Perez was in a wheelchair and still in pain, but did not say whether the family had decided that he should undergo surgery. The Department of Homeland Security has said Garces Perez, who has been taken to a hospital twice since the shooting, is receiving around-the-clock medical care and pain medication.
“If they want to say it’s great medical care, they should start providing great medical care today by having him leave the detention center, go to a hospital or to a doctor, and do not delay his surgery if that’s what his family chooses to do,” Casar said.
Casar, whose district includes Austin, was the first member of Congress to visit Garces Perez in person since the shooting. He said the wound in Garces Perez’s back remains bloody and medical staff change his gauze two or three times daily.
Following Casar’s visit and a press conference, DHS issued a previous statement denying claims that Garces Perez was forced to sleep on a floor or that he was prevented from having the bullet removed, saying ICE would not advise on a medical procedure for a detainee.
Garces Perez was making a DoorDash delivery when ICE officers in an unmarked truck sideswiped his car twice, his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said. He was shot and taken to a hospital, then released into ICE custody with a bullet still in his back, she said.
ICE and DHS haven’t said what led to the shooting beyond that Garces Perez was “the subject of a targeted vehicle stop.”
ICE has not said if the agent who fired was wearing a body camera. At the beginning of September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he expected all field agents to have them by the end of the month.
Austin police released body camera footage from its officers who arrived just after the shooting. Garces Perez is seen hunched over in the front seat of his car and grabbing his shoulder and rocking back and forth. An officer later cut off Garces Perez’s shirt, and a wound can be seen in his upper back.
Garces Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to make appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day in office.
Garces Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to Lincoln-Goldfinch. She said a judge issued a deportation order after Garces Perez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.
Garces Perez’s shooting came at the end of a summer in which ICE notably ramped up enforcement operations in Austin and surrounding suburbs and increasingly targeted immigrants without criminal records in public places.
In all, ICE made more than 1,000 arrests in Austin, Pflugerville and other nearby cities during June and July, more than an 80% increase from a year earlier, which had been the previous peak, according to ICE data provided to the Deportation Data Project at the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of California, Los Angeles, and analyzed by The Associated Press.
Unlike some other places, the increases in Austin were not driven by partnerships with local law enforcement agencies or by picking up jail inmates. Instead, the data shows that ICE officers made the vast majority of arrests in the community through traffic stops and other enforcement methods.
Nearly 2 out of 3 people who were arrested in the Austin area had no criminal convictions and no pending criminal charges, the data shows.
