articles.title_orig: 'The Best-Sounding Headphones We've Ever Built': Beats President Talks Beats 360, Customization, And Apple
articles.title_zh: 'The Best-Sounding Headphones We've Ever Built': Beats President Talks Beats 360, Customization, And Apple
articles.content_orig:
A few hours after Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo in Cupertino, California, BGR attended a hands-on experience just miles away for another major new release: the Beats 360 headphones. The new over-ear headphones are the most versatile product we've seen from the company, with powerful sound, impressive comfort, and plenty of style. In addition to reviewing the Beats 360 , we also had a chance to speak with Oliver Schusser, Beats President and Apple Music VP, who previously spoke to us about the Powerbeats Fit lineup . This time around, we discussed the latest headphones, the relationship between Beats and Apple, and the future of the company's accessory lineups.
What's most interesting about Beats 360 is how much they differ from most anything we've seen from Beats in the past. With a focus on customization, there are over 256 combinations from day one that users can choose from. You might never see another pair that looks exactly like yours. "It's only been a few years since we brought out Studio Pro," Schusser noted, "but we wanted to create a different kind of over-ear product that caters a different use case, which is the active lifestyle."
According to Schusser, Beats noticed how many people have started wearing over-ear headphones to go to the gym. Beats saw an opening. With this release, Beats combined breathable materials, a tight grip, and an experience more similar to earbuds in a pair of over-ear headphones.
While the iPhone Duo represents a new era for the iPhone, Beats is going through a similar shift with Beats 360. While the company took the category by storm when it entered the market in 2008, this is an opportunity to chart a new path forward alongside its parent company.
Besides that, these Beats headphones sound great, and even though the company chose not to use Apple's proprietary audio chips, the sound is crisp, clear, and powerful. "It's a case-by-case decision which chip we use," Schusser tells BGR. "What's important for us is that we want to be optimized for both iOS and Android. With this chip, users can have personalized Spatial Audio, and Android users can have the full feature set as well."
One of the unique features of the Beats 360 headphones is the ability to replace the ear cushions and headband. Customers can choose between four different frames, eight cushions (in both a breathable performance knit and UltraPlush options), and eight different headbands. To celebrate the release, Beats is offering these add-on accessories for $9.99 , but they will eventually climb to $49.99 each.
During the interview, I asked Schusser about the relationship between Apple and Beats. After all, Beats 360 sounds great, but they make a few compromises — no auto-play/pause functionality, no Live Translation, and no support for Lossless capabilities, which was something Beats added before Apple. Even when Beats is first to introduce a feature, like the heart-rate sensor available on the Powerbeats Pro 2 , the functionality was only fully supported by the iPhone once Apple released AirPods Pro 3 with the same feature a few months later. It gives the impression that Apple wants to be sure AirPods will always take priority.
Still, Schusser tells me that in the organization the teams are the same, and these decisions are all very conscious. "It's all about what we want the product to be, what price point we want it to be at," he says. "We also want to make sure our headphones work just as great on both iOS and Android platforms. Still, everyone at Apple is proud to have Beats, and everyone at Beats is proud to be part of Apple. Customers can choose between AirPods and Beats, and the good thing is they coexist side-by-side in a beautiful way."
Asked about cases, which have been absent from this year's iPhone 18 Pro release, Schusser confirms that Beats is, for now, stepping away from that business." We've had two iPhone cycles of cases. We've actually learned a lot and we've decided not to make any cases this year. However, one of the things that has worked extremely well for us is cables. They're super popular, and we plan to add even more colors to them." Schusser also teases that there's even more to come from Beats, which means the company might not be completely done with releasing new accessories.

articles.title_orig: Trump threatens Iran, predicts Cuba's fall. Key UN takeaways
articles.title_zh: Trump threatens Iran, predicts Cuba's fall. Key UN takeaways
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump made multiple false claims in his address to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, though he largely stuck to a prepared text.
Here is a fact check of some of his assertions.
Trump, repeating a frequent false claim, said, “Since I took office, it has been my great honor to settle eight wars.”
He specified that he was talking about conflicts between Cambodia and Thailand; Kosovo and Serbia; Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo; India and Pakistan; Armenia and Azerbaijan; and the war in Gaza. And he has previously claimed that the other two wars he ended were last year’s brief conflict between Israel and Iran and a supposed war between Egypt and Ethiopia.
Trump’s “eight” figure is a clear exaggeration.
His list includes two situations that were never actually wars during his tenure. The situation between Egypt and Ethiopia was a diplomatic dispute over an Ethiopian dam project, not a war, and the mysterious supposed issue he says he resolved between Serbia and Kosovo was also not a war.
In addition, the war involving Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo has not ended despite a peace agreement brokered by the Trump administration. And though Trump cited the war in Gaza, Israel continues to conduct frequent attacks in the enclave despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Trump did help to end the brief 2025 conflict between Israel and Iran, though Israel proceeded to join the US in starting another war against Iran in 2026.
Trump scoffed at dire warnings that artificial intelligence might eventually attack or kill people, claiming they are coming from “the very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming, a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead.”
There are at least four things wrong with his sentence about global warming.
First, the phrase “global warming” remains in widespread use even though the phrase “climate change” is also common; they mean different things. Climate scientists use both, often saying “global warming” when referring to the long-term trend of increasing global temperature and “climate change” when referring to the numerous effects the world is experiencing because of that trend. (NASA, part of the Trump-led federal government, explains the difference between the terms on its website.) For example, a 2023 report from the UN’s climate change panel is titled “Climate Change 2023: Synthesis Report,” but it says this: “Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming, with global surface temperature reaching 1.1°C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020.”
Second, while Trump didn’t say what time period he was talking about, he didn’t acknowledge that the world has continued to get warmer, not cooler. The UN’s World Meteorological Organization reported in January that “the past 11 years have been the 11 warmest on record,” with 2023, 2024 and 2025 the three very warmest — as NASA also found — though 2025 wasn’t as hot as 2024.
Third, experts widely disagree that “nobody” has died from the various impacts of a warming world. It’s impossible to pinpoint a precise death number, but some estimates total in the millions. The deaths are likely to continue; the World Health Organization says , “Between 2030 and 2050, climate change is expected to cause approximately 250,000 additional deaths per year, from undernutrition, malaria, diarrhea and heat stress alone.”
Fourth, while somebody somewhere might have said that “we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming,” that isn’t how an expert report framed the issue.
A widely discussed 2018 report from climate scientists said the world needed to sharply cut carbon emissions within the next 12 years to be on track to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels; scientists said above that threshold, the potential deadly impacts from climate change would be larger . Though the 2018 report was often oversimplified by politicians, the expert claim was never that “we’ll all be dead in 12 years” — it was that significant action was needed within 12 years to improve the future. (The UN program reported earlier this month that the world is set to exceed the 1.5-degree increase, “likely within the next few years.”)
Trump delivered a more cautious version of his inaccurate previous boast that $21 trillion in investment is pouring into the US, this time saying, “We’ve secured commitments for $21 trillion in new investments from all over the planet.” His figure has no apparent basis even with the “secured commitments for” caveat; the White House has never been able to substantiate it.
When the president spoke at the UN, the White House’s own website claimed there had been “$11.2 trillion” in “major investment announcements” during Trump’s second term, far less than the “$21 trillion” in commitments the president cited. And a detailed CNN review in 2025 found the White House list was counting trillions in vague investment pledges, pledges that were about “bilateral trade” or “economic exchange” rather than investment in the US, and vague statements that didn’t even rise to the level of pledges.
The White House figure includes pledges from US-based companies as well as foreign entities. Federal data shows that new foreign direct investment in the US was about $232 billion in 2025.
Trump defended the Iran war at length. And he claimed, “The cowards and traitors would love to say the United States is low on munitions, but that’s not true. We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we’re building them at levels that we have never done before.”
We don’t have access to classified information on the precise current state of US munitions stockpiles, and it’s not clear who Trump is calling “cowards and traitors.” But it’s not just CNN and other media outlets that have reported that the war with Iran has depleted at least some US munitions levels; the federal inspector general overseeing the Defense Department and the nonpartisan federal Congressional Budget Office essentially said the same in separate reports released last week.
The inspector general report, which discussed the period from the beginning of April through the end of June, said a Defense Department acquisitions office “said that the munitions expenditure in (the war) has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
The report said the acquisitions office also noted that while the Pentagon “has begun to implement mitigation strategies, the defense industrial base requires ‘significant lead time’ to expand production capacities.” The report specified: “The most persistent bottlenecks remain in the production of solid rocket motors, the availability of high-grade explosives and propellants, and the recruitment of skilled manufacturing labor.”
The Congressional Budget Office report said there is a “shortfall” of missile defense interceptors and that the war will leave “the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years.” The report said the Defense Department had a “limited” inventory of interceptors even before Israel and the US attacked Iran during a brief conflict in June 2025, and that the budget office’s research indicates the US “has probably used between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of those munitions since June 2025.”
“Given the number of missile defense interceptors that DoD has recently used, their currently low production rates, and the historical difficulty of scaling up their production, rebuilding DoD’s inventory of interceptors would probably take at least five years — even if production was increased,” the report said.
The Defense Department has consistently said it’s not true that there are any munitions shortfalls, and it did so again last week.

articles.title_orig: US-China Summit begins with signs that the trade truce will stay in place — for now
articles.title_zh: US-China Summit begins with signs that the trade truce will stay in place — for now
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. and China have extended a truce to keep tariffs lower for longer and rare earths flowing, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday local time.
He was speaking on Fox News, as Chinese President Xi Jinping landed in Washington, D.C. for a state visit through Friday.
Xi and Trump agreed to a one-year trade truce at a meeting in South Korea last October. The deal, which was set to expire in November, will now be extended to Jan. 10, Bessent said. He added that Beijing needs to fulfill more deliverables.
Ahead of this week's summit, many had expected the truce would be extended by six months or longer.
The U.S. and China should discuss their differences on trade issues on the basis of mutual benefit, without actively imposing restrictions, said Dong Shaopeng, senior researcher at Renmin University of China. He expected the trade truce could be continually improved and extended.
Chinese state media did not immediately note Bessent's comments on the trade truce.
The two-month extension "suggests to me the U.S. is unsatisfied with China's offers and wants to keep the heat on, with a bonus being it is more likely that Xi goes to the G20 in Miami," said Scott Kennedy of the U.S.-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump visited Beijing in May. The two leaders could also meet alongside an APEC meeting in Shenzhen in November, and the G20 summit in Miami in December.
However, Jens Eskelund, president of the European Chamber of Commerce in China, pointed out that simply extending the trade truce does not address challenges companies face, including the lack of a standardized approach to apply for rare earths export licenses.
Xi said in an official readout for his arrival that he is confident the visit will produce "fruitful results" for both sides. He said the two countries should be partners, not rivals, and work to build a stable relationship where competition and differences are managed. The readout did not mention tariffs, rare earths or artificial intelligence.
Footage streamed on China's state broadcaster showed U.S. President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump meeting Xi and First Lady of China Peng Liyuan at the foot of the Chinese leader's jet. The video did not show the U.S. and Chinese leaders shaking hands — it focused on Xi and his wife shaking hands with two children presenting them each with bouquets.
After greeting Xi, Trump told reporters he would discuss the Iran war with the Chinese leader, among "many other subjects."
Bessent met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York ahead of Xi's arrival in the U.S. The two sides discussed setting up an alert system for AI incidents , according to Bessent.
While executives of major U.S. tech companies plan to join a summit dinner on Thursday , none of their Chinese counterparts are expected to attend.
Politburo Standing Committee Member Cai Qi and China's top diplomat Wang Yi accompanied Xi, according to state media.
—CNBC's Eunice Yoon and Ashlee Trujillo contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump hails ‘truly great friendship’ with Xi Jinping as the Chinese leader begins his state visit
articles.title_zh: Trump hails ‘truly great friendship’ with Xi Jinping as the Chinese leader begins his state visit
articles.content_orig:
They are expected to discuss AI safety, Taiwan, trade and the Iran war.
President Donald Trump greeted Chinese President Xi Jinping in a lavish ceremony at the White House on Thursday as the leaders are set for a day of meetings and a state dinner in a high-stakes visit.
The two leaders are expected to discuss a number of issues, including artificial intelligence safety, Taiwan, trade, the Iran war and critical minerals during their bilateral meeting on Thursday.
Ahead of the private meeting between the two geopolitical rivals, Trump touted the "truly great friendship" between the two leaders, while Xi delivered pointed remarks on trade and AI.
"From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people," Trump said from a podium in the Grand Foyer of the White House.
Trump commented on the historic nature of Thursday's state visit, as Xi has not visited the White House in more than a decade. Xi last visited the White House in a 2015 state visit during the Obama administration.
"Melania and I are honored to host you in Washington as President Xi becomes the first ever Chinese leader to make a second formal state visit to America," Trump said.
"During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology and super intelligence. The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," Trump said.
Trump also touted the "tremendous strides" the two leaders have made, with the president pointing to continued work on creating "a more balanced trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers."
The president made no explicit mention of Iran during his remarks Thursday morning -- even as China continues to offer support to Iran amid the conflict with the United States.
Speaking after Trump, President Xi thanked his U.S. counterpart for the "warm hospitality," and said "there is plenty of room for us to work together," later stressing the importance of healthy competition, according to a consecutive translation of his remarks.
"We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses," Xi said via translation.
Xi emphasized the importance of ensuring that Chinese companies are being "treated fairly" in the U.S., notable remarks given the tit-for-tat trade war the two countries have engaged in.
"China-U.S. cooperation may not solve every problem in the world, but without our cooperation, it would be hard to solve many of the world's problems. China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies wanting to invest and do business there. We hope Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States," Xi said.
Xi also directly addressed the issue of AI, saying that both countries have the ability and duty to make sure AI remains under human control.
"Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence. We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people," Xi said via translation.
Xi also emphasized his eagerness to work with Trump and similarly nodded to their warm relationship.
"China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust. President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch," he said.
At the conclusion of his remarks, Xi shared that two giant pandas will be coming to the U.S.-- an announcement that prompted a smile from Trump.
"The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans. Here, I have a piece of good news. In a few days, two pandas, Ping-Ping and Fu Shuang, will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta, and meet with the American people," Xi said.
Later Thursday, Xi and his wife will be the guests of honor when Trump and the first lady host the Chinese delegation for a state dinner in the East Room, where both leaders are expected to deliver remarks.
Guests scheduled to attend the state dinner include tech executives such as Amazon's founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai of Google and Michael Dell, the CEO of Dell Technologies, the White House and a source familiar told ABC News.
Also on the guest list are Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Jane Fraser, the CEO of Citigroup, and Tim Cook, who recently stepped down as the CEO of Apple.
On Friday, Xi and his wife are scheduled to join Trump and the first lady for a private tea and a tour of the National Archives to view historical national documents. Xi is expected to depart the U.S. later Friday.

Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
Trump-Xi summit – latest updates
Xi Jingping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course.
At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could avoid military conflict between the two competing superpowers.
“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialog, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.
“We should coexist in peace,” he said. “China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”
With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.
Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.
His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.
Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was US president.
Trump declared that he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”
He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: China to send 2 giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta, President Xi Jinping says: "Envoy of friendship"
articles.title_zh: China to send 2 giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta, President Xi Jinping says: "Envoy of friendship"
articles.content_orig:
Chinese President Xi Jinping announced some panda diplomacy on Thursday during a meeting with President Trump and other White House officials, saying that two pandas are an "envoy of friendship."
The short announcement was the latest update since the Atlanta zoo announced a new research agreement with the China Wildlife Conservation Association. As part of that agreement, the organization expects to send over male panda Ping Ping and female panda Fu Shuang, from the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
"We can't wait to meet Ping Ping and Fu Shuang and to welcome our members, guests, city, and community back to the wonder and joy of giant pandas," the zoo's president, Raymond B. King, said in a statement in April.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that the new round of cooperation on conservation would help improve the health and well-being of the giant pandas, advance global biodiversity protection and strengthen the friendship between the Chinese and American people.
During an earlier giant panda agreement between the zoo and China that concluded in 2024, pandas Lun Lun and Yang Yang gave birth to seven bears, the zoo said. Lun Lun and Yang Yang and their two youngest offspring left Atlanta for China in October 2024, where the rest of their offspring reside.
Details about when Ping Ping and Fu Shuang may arrive in Atlanta remain limited. A spokesperson for the zoo told CBS News Atlanta that they would not be sharing the date at this time. In the meantime, zoo officials say they were carrying out facility upgrades, among other preparation work, to create a more comfortable and safer environment for the pair with technical guidance from Chinese experts.
Giant pandas have been a symbol of the U.S.-China friendship ever since Beijing gifted a pair of pandas to the National Zoo in Washington, D.C. in 1972, and China has long used its giant panda loan program as a tool of Beijing's soft power diplomacy worldwide.
Currently, two zoos in the United States have pandas. The National Zoo and the San Diego Zoo both received pandas from China in 2024.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

Myles McCormick in Washington
Published September 24 2026
This is an on-site version of the White House Watch newsletter. You can read the previous edition here . Sign up for free here to get it on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Email us at [email protected]
Hello from Washington and welcome to White House Watch. On our agenda today:
Trump and Xi meet in Washington for pivotal summit
Influencer Hasan Piker says Republican efforts to vilify him are falling short
Republicans are splashing out on midterm election advertising
All eyes are on Washington today, where Xi Jinping has arrived for a high-stakes two-day summit with Donald Trump (Follow along with the FT’s live blog here ).
It is the Chinese president’s first visit to the US capital in more than a decade. And as my colleagues Demetri Sevastopulo and Joe Leahy report , it will involve plenty of fanfare.
At the top of the agenda are trade relations and the creation of an AI dialogue to discuss risks posed by the technology. Shortly after Xi landed last night, US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said the countries had agreed to extend their one-year trade truce, which was set to expire on November 10, until January 10.
Xi is also expected to raise the subject of Taiwan. Trump sparked alarm in May when he said American arms sales to Taiwan were a “good negotiating chip” , suggesting that he might curtail US support for Taipei.
But there will also be plenty of pomp and cultural events. A formal welcome ceremony will be held on the South Lawn of the White House this morning, featuring a military review and flyover by fighter jets and bombers.
In the evening, the pair will be joined by their wives and a host of Big Tech and Wall Street executives for an official state dinner. On the guest list are Tesla boss Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, Jane Fraser from Citigroup and Apple’s former chief Tim Cook.
In a statement issued after his arrival last night, Xi said it was a “great pleasure” to pay a state visit to the US. The two countries should be “partners, not rivals”, the Chinese leader said, adding that 2026 was a “pivotal” year for US-China relations.
Trump’s show of respect for his Chinese counterpart underlines the shift from his aggressive stance towards Beijing during his first term — an approach that has frustrated the ambitions of the hawks in his administration .
But the US president’s changeable nature and willingness to deploy tariffs as a geopolitical weapon mean nothing is certain in the relationship. Amid all the fanfare of the next two days, the world will be watching attentively.

Republicans are far outspending Democrats on advertising ahead of November 3’s midterm elections, reserving roughly $1bn in advertising slots between September 1 and election day, according to an FT analysis.
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to temporarily restore White House access to CNN, MS Now and Politico after the news outlets had been banned by the president.
A global bond rout has deepened as oil jumped back above $105 a barrel on Thursday, adding to inflation fears after the US Treasury market suffered its biggest fall since last year’s trade war sell-off. The US oil industry also warned there was no “silver bullet” solution to the supply crunch.
Belgium’s foreign ministry has warned internally that the US under Trump is no longer a reliable ally , according to a document seen by the FT.
The UK is reviewing its plan to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, after Trump renewed his opposition to the deal in a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Leftwing influencer Hasan Piker was accused by House Speaker Mike Johnson this month of wanting to lead the US down a “dark, dangerous, deadly road to communism”.
But the prolific Twitch streamer — seen by many on the right as one of the most dangerous men in the country — told my colleague Guy Chazan that Republicans’ campaign of vilification “isn’t working”.
“If you talk to me you very quickly realise I’m a fairly pragmatic person,” he told the FT, adding that the Financial Times was his “favourite newspaper”.
Piker is a self-declared “socialist anti-imperialist” who once said America “deserved 9/11” (for which he later apologised) and has enraged supporters of Israel by saying that he would “vote for Hamas over Israel every time”. He was also banned in June from entering the UK because his presence “may not be conducive to the public good”.
In an interview with the FT, the bogeyman of the Republican Party hit back at attempts to brand him a “dangerous, radical, Islamist, jihadist terrorist”.
“A lot of these manosphere guys don’t know what they’re talking about — their level of involvement with politics is super, super basic,” Piker said.
Donald Trump’s proposed diesel export ban will backfire , according to Lex’s Camilla Palladino.
Martin Wolf says the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates in spite of Trump’s demands was “sensible” and “overdue” .
Calling for closer EU-Canada ties without pooling sovereignty is an abdication of European responsibility , argues Martin Sandbu.
As Germany’s Friedrich Merz comes under pressure and speculation grows over who could succeed him at the helm of Europe’s biggest economy, Janan Ganesh maintains the west does not have a leadership problem .
While existential fears over technology rise, the FT editorial board says the US and China can work together on AI security .

Two giant pandas from China will arrive at Zoo Atlanta in the coming days, renewing a loan initiative that had lapsed amid diplomatic friction between Beijing and Washington.
Chinese President Xi Jinping confirmed the timeline Thursday after China and the facility said in April that Ping Ping, a male, and Fu Shuang, a female, would travel to the United States.
Xi’s White House statement before talks with President Donald Trump offered the first public confirmation of the schedule. Beijing had recalled four pandas from Atlanta in 2024, ending the last active U.S. panda loans at the time.
Xi said Ping Ping and Fu Shuang "will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people" in "a few days." He described the update as "a piece of good news" and celebrated the program as showing "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."
The animals arrive under a conservation agreement between the zoo and the China Wildlife Conservation Association. Both pandas were born at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding in China.
In 2024, Lun Lun, Yang Yang, Ya Lun, and Xi Lun returned from Zoo Atlanta to China, concluding a 25-year arrangement and leaving the U.S. without any pandas for several months. The National Zoo in Washington sent back three pandas in 2023, receiving Bao Li and Qing Bao in October 2024. Other U.S. facilities previously returned pandas as agreements lapsed.
When Atlanta's pandas were officially promised in the spring, Zoo Atlanta CEO Raymond B. King welcomed "the wonder and joy of giant pandas" and said the zoo was "delighted and honored to yet again be trusted as stewards of this treasured species."

articles.title_orig: Xi says 2 giant pandas from China will arrive in the coming days at Atlanta’s zoo
articles.title_zh: Xi says 2 giant pandas from China will arrive in the coming days at Atlanta’s zoo
articles.content_orig:
Chinese President Xi Jinping announced some panda diplomacy on Thursday during a meeting with President Trump and other White House officials, saying that two pandas are an "envoy of friendship."
The short announcement was the latest update since the Atlanta zoo announced a new research agreement with the China Wildlife Conservation Association. As part of that agreement, the organization expects to send over male panda Ping Ping and female panda Fu Shuang, from the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
"We can't wait to meet Ping Ping and Fu Shuang and to welcome our members, guests, city, and community back to the wonder and joy of giant pandas," the zoo's president, Raymond B. King, said in a statement in April.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that the new round of cooperation on conservation would help improve the health and well-being of the giant pandas, advance global biodiversity protection and strengthen the friendship between the Chinese and American people.
During an earlier giant panda agreement between the zoo and China that concluded in 2024, pandas Lun Lun and Yang Yang gave birth to seven bears, the zoo said. Lun Lun and Yang Yang and their two youngest offspring left Atlanta for China in October 2024, where the rest of their offspring reside.
Details about when Ping Ping and Fu Shuang may arrive in Atlanta remain limited. A spokesperson for the zoo told CBS News Atlanta that they would not be sharing the date at this time. In the meantime, zoo officials say they were carrying out facility upgrades, among other preparation work, to create a more comfortable and safer environment for the pair with technical guidance from Chinese experts.
Giant pandas have been a symbol of the U.S.-China friendship ever since Beijing gifted a pair of pandas to the National Zoo in Washington, D.C. in 1972, and China has long used its giant panda loan program as a tool of Beijing's soft power diplomacy worldwide.
Currently, two zoos in the United States have pandas. The National Zoo and the San Diego Zoo both received pandas from China in 2024.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Sorna CEO on AI race: You can’t understand the intensity of innovation in China unless you’re there
articles.title_zh: Sorna CEO on AI race: You can’t understand the intensity of innovation in China unless you’re there
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING—China's Commerce Ministry confirmed Thursday that its senior trade negotiators had held their first talks with the U.S. on artificial intelligence.
Spokesperson He Yadong told reporters the two sides also discussed plans for reducing tariffs, and extending trade arrangements agreed in Kuala Lumpur last October.
He was referring to China's Vice Premier He Lifeng meeting with his counterpart, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in New York in the runup to the summit this week between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As Xi landed in the U.S., Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday the two countries agreed to extend a trade truce to January. The truce, reached in October 2025, kept tariffs lower and limited China's export controls on rare earths, which are critical components of semiconductors and many household goods, as well as defense products.
Earlier in the week, Bessent said the two sides discussed establishing an AI dialogue and a mechanism to alert each other about AI risks.
The Chinese confirmation of the AI talks came just hours before Xi and Trump were scheduled to begin talks in Washington, D.C., as part of a state visit.
Trump said in a Truth Social post early Thursday that the leaders would discuss AI.
"A big day with President Xi of China. Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!" he wrote.
The president has been vocal about his opposition to further regulation of AI and reiterated his position to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that: "We're going to encourage it, not rein it in."
The ministry added the two sides held constructive, candid talks, and reached multiple points of consensus.
Both countries are weighing how to address the risks posed by rapidly advancing technology after recent incidents involving AI systems raised fears that increasingly autonomous models could make attacks faster and harder to contain.

articles.title_orig: Hitler's possible role in niece's death under scrutiny after documents raise questions about alibi, report says
articles.title_zh: Hitler's possible role in niece's death under scrutiny after documents raise questions about alibi, report says
articles.content_orig:
Newly unearthed records in a Munich archive have cast doubt on Adolf Hitler's whereabouts at the time of his niece's suspicious 1931 death, according to news magazine Der Spiegel.
Hitler's unusually close and controlling relationship with his niece, Geli Raubal, has long been the subject of speculation and rumor, and newspaper reports at the time suggested that Hitler may have played a role in her death.
Raubal died from a gunshot wound to the chest from a pistol belonging to Hitler, in what was officially determined to be a suicide.
According to the official account, Hitler's personal servant, Georg Winter, discovered the 23-year-old Raubal's body on the floor inside her locked room in Hitler's apartment in Munich on Sept. 19, 1931, a Saturday.
Hitler, who at the time was a prominent far-right extremist but had not yet seized power in Germany, was away in the city of Nuremberg that day, giving him what appeared to be a strong alibi.
But according to an article in Der Spiegel , historian Harald Sandner recently discovered documents in archives in Munich casting doubt on that account — and raising questions about whether Nazi sympathizers in the police may have falsified records to protect Hitler.
Two death notices and an entry in an official local death registry all put the date of the discovery of Raubal's body to Sept. 18, a full day earlier, when Hitler was known to still have been in Munich.
Hitler's relationship with Raubal, the daughter of his half-sister Angela Raubal, was the subject of intense speculation. Some contemporaries believed Hitler had been abusive or had pursued a sexual relationship with his relative.
Hitler reportedly strictly controlled nearly every aspect of Raubal's life after she moved to Munich in 1927.
She reportedly argued intensely with Hitler just before her death after Hitler refused to allow her to move to Vienna.
Sandner told the magazine the discrepancy in the documents over the date of Raubal's death may point toward a cover-up by the police, though there is no decisive proof.
Days after Raubal's death, a left-wing Munich newspaper reported Hitler had been in a heated argument with his niece, that injuries had been found on her body and that Nazi officials held crisis meetings regarding how to present the matter to the public.
Other newspapers suggested Hitler might have had Raubal killed — or killed her himself — though the Nazi leader publicly denied those allegations in a statement.

A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to immediately restore White House access for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico journalists after the President issued a media ban last week.
In a District of Columbia court, Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order of 14 days against the ban, saying it “likely violated” the media outlets’ “constitutional due process rights.” The order came in response to a lawsuit filed against the Trump Administration by CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday, in which the outlets argued the ban was a “direct assault” on the First Amendment and violated their Fifth Amendment due process rights.
In a significant setback for Trump, the court ordered that journalists from the banned media outlets should have their White House access reinstated “until further order of the court or the expiration of this temporary restraining order.” In a statement to TIME, Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, said “this is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
TIME has approached the White House and Justice Department for comment.
Outlining his ruling, Kelly said the outlets had “shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim.” The Fifth Amendment protects Americans from being “deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.” Kelly determined that the outlets were “likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process.”
The judge also rejected the Trump Administration's assertion that the media ​ban was motivated by “national security” concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the WhiteHouse—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote, referencing Trump’s “fake news” reasoning .
The Justice Department, in a legal filing on Tuesday, said the outlets had “received adequate notice” of the ban (a point contested by Kelly) and insisted “the President’s actions are lawful under the First Amendment.”
There has been an outpouring of solidarity among other media outlets in light of the ban.
CNN, one of five U.S. news outlets in the White House press pool that rotates responsibility for pooled live video coverage, was scheduled to cover Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday. When they were restricted from doing so, other major television networks declined to replace CNN’s pool crew.
In a rare joint statement, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said : “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No Administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
In a further show of support, some media publications—including the New York Times and Washington Post —announced they would hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage.
On Wednesday, 49 media organizations filed a legal brief voicing their support of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. “Stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of Supreme Court jurisprudence and is impermissible in any type of forum, including the White House,” the brief argued.
Ahead of Thursday’s order, Trump dismissed the legal challenge and indicated he regretted appointing Judge Kelly in 2017.
Vowing to fight any legal block on his ban, Trump insisted : “Almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal, because fake news people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our national security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the [Oval Office].”
However, in the court filing, Kelly has stated that “temporary restraining orders are generally unappealable.”
Instead, during the 14-day period, the court “will set a schedule for expedited briefing on a motion for a preliminary injunction,” allowing Trump and the media outlets to submit further evidence for Kelly to consider.
Trump has a turbulent history with the media. In 2018, he revoked the White House press credentials of Jim Acosta, who was then a CNN correspondent, after a tense exchange during a news conference.
CNN challenged the decision in court and it was Judge Kelly who ordered the White House to reinstate the reporter’s press pass.

The government of Yemen is seeking U.S. military support in its fight against the Houthis , a senior Yemeni official said Wednesday, as the Iranian-backed rebels rapidly expand their control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and threaten another critical Middle East waterway for global energy supplies.
Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, conveyed the request for U.S. assistance to President Donald Trump in a call this week, Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice president of the Yemeni Leadership Council, told reporters on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly .
Asked about a report this week by Reuters, which cited one Yemeni and one Western source as saying Trump made no direct pledge of military support during the call, Bawazir said he was unaware that the request had been rejected.
He said that Trump understands the danger of the Houthis and that “we hope and expect more support for the Yemeni government in the face of the Houthi militias.”
The White House did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment overnight.
Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital
Bawazir did not say whether U.S. support should extend to direct military strikes.
“We do not ask the American soldiers to actually go into war on our behalf,” he said. “And we don’t really request that they do nothing.”
Yemen does look forward to “mutual coordination on the intel and security fields,” according to Bawazir, who requested that the U.S. enhance the Yemeni government’s own military capacity to take on the threat.
“The aerial campaigns are important,” he said. “But supporting the Yemeni government and forces on the ground is indeed a guarantor to end the danger of those militias.”
Yemen has been embroiled in various states of conflict since 2014, when the Houthis drove the internationally recognized government out of the capital city, Sanaa, and ignited a regional proxy war, with Saudi Arabia supporting the exiled government against the Iranian-backed rebels.
In their latest military campaign, the Houthis have advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline with the aim of cutting off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which has become a critical waterway for Saudi Arabia to transport oil after Iran effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz .
Saudi Arabia, a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including in the U.S. war with Iran, has urged the U.S. to take military action against the Houthis, who further escalated their actions over the weekend by launching an attack on the Saudi capital, Riyadh . So far U.S. support has been limited to providing intelligence and targeting data.
Trump, who announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group, went so far as to order strikes against the Houthis on Sunday, NBC News has reported , but the order was canceled hours later.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that the U.S. has made commitments to the Saudis and is living up to them, adding that “obviously, the president has many options available to him.”
Trump said this month that the Houthis, which the U.S. designates as a terrorist organization, don’t want to fight the U.S. and “they don’t want us to go after them.”
“They’ve called and they’ve talked to us, and they don’t want us to,” Trump told reporters while he was in Ireland. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.”
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told The Associated Press on Sunday that it was the U.S. that had reached out to the rebel group after its advancement toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
“We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy,” al-Bukhaiti said. “And that remains the case.”
Bawazir warned it would be a mistake to accept assurances from a group that is “connected to a deviant state in the region,” referring to Iran, as it may be seen as legitimizing the Houthis. But he said Yemen was comfortable with the U.S. position.
“We do indeed discuss this particular issue very, very deeply,” he said.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.title_orig: Macklemore Announces Free Palestine Tour
articles.title_zh: Macklemore Announces Free Palestine Tour
articles.content_orig:
Macklemore announced he will launch the Free Palestine Tour this fall after being removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour this month over his pro-Palestinian performance .
The “Thrift Shop” rapper took to Instagram on Monday and jokingly said that his “schedule freed up a bit,” announcing three performance dates in Dublin, London and Paris next month.
“What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage,” he wrote. “When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”
The performances are part of what Macklemore named the “Free Palestine” tour and the poster said it would be him “and friends.” He said he spent the last week reaching out to other artists to work out scheduling, but no other names have been announced as of Monday.
He wrote that there has been a “been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation” and the expectations of artists.
“It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore,” Macklemore said. “People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community.”
All proceeds from the performances would benefit organizations supporting Palestinians, he said.
Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, announced earlier this month that U.S. venues gave Sheeran an ultimatum to remove him from the tour or face show cancelations. Macklemore said that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft “rallied” other stadium owners after taking issue with his “Free Palestine” remarks during a show.
Sheeran confirmed that Kraft was among those who called him after Macklemore performed his anti-war song and the speech that preceded it at Metlife Stadium circulated online.
The situation surrounding Macklemore, Sheeran and Kraft made international headlines this month as many debated not just Macklemore’s speech regarding the Israel-Gaza war, but also the rights for artists to express their views.
It began when Macklemore joined Sheeran’s “Loop” tour in New Jersey and performed “Hind’s Hall,” his song inspired by the anti-war protests at Columbia University in 2024. Macklemore made a speech prior to the performance that called for a “Free Palestine” and also told Jewish members of the audience that his comments regarding the Israeli government was in no way about them. The performance of “Hind’s Hall” also had related images from pro-Palestinian demonstrations and the situation in Gaza.
Kraft did not deny allegations made by Macklemore in his own statement earlier this month, but said Gillette Stadium — which his entertainment group owns — seeks to create a welcoming environment for everyone. He took issue with Macklemore’s actions at the New Jersey show and “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.”
“Much of my time and attention for the last decade has been focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed,” Kraft said.
The Patriots owner also said he was not trying to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminish the suffering of Palestinians.
Kraft did not specifically reference past actions of concern from Macklemore, but many online brought up a 2014 incident in which Macklemore wore a costume that appeared to play on antisemitic tropes: a wig, a fake beard and a hooked nose. He wore it to the Grammys that year, saying at the time that he thought it would be fun to dress in disguise to talk to fans.
Macklemore apologized after the antisemitic stereotype was pointed out, saying he had been in touch with the Anti-Defamation League, an organization founded to combat antisemitism. The ADL accepted the apology at the time, saying it took him “at his word that he did not have any ill intent,” according to The Guardian .
Sheeran faced a wave of backlash over his role in the situation as some commenters felt that the singer should have taken a stance on the war or at least Macklemore’s right to speak on his opinion. All of Sheeran’s opening acts, as well as his house band, dropped out of their scheduled U.S. tour dates in solidarity with Macklemore and the Palestinian people.
The “Perfect” singer initially released a statement explaining his side of the situation and clarifying that it was not his choice to drop Macklemore. Sheeran said that his promoters, who held the contract with Macklemore, made the decision as he attempted to build bridges with venue owners.
Sheeran went on with his scheduled concert in Philadelphia on Saturday, tearfully addressing the crowd who showed up in spite of the criticism he faced.
“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said. “But this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”
Israel launched its offensive in the Gaza Strip after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and roughly 250 others were taken hostage. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Gaza during Israel’s military campaign, including at least 1,200 since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.
Sheeran acknowledged the “horrific” Oct. 7 attack on Israel by Hamas which started the war, but went on to say what has happened in Gaza as a result is “catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate.”
“This is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore,” he said.

Oracle shares fell 5% on Thursday following news that the company sent a "force majeure" notice tied to its New Mexico data center project to protect itself from higher expenses.
"Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule," an Oracle said in a statement to CNBC. "We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward."
Bloomberg was first to report the news, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The company is looking to delay payment on the campus, dubbed Project Jupiter, if it doesn't come online as expected in 2028, according to the report.
Oracle sent the notice to the developer, which is a unit of Blue Owl Capital , CNBC confirmed. Blue Owl also saw its shares fall on Thursday.
"This notice does not change the financial commitments to this multi-year project," Blue Owl Capital said in a statement to CNBC.
The New Mexico data center project, which is part of the broader Stargate artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout with President Donald Trump , has been riddled with setbacks and regulatory hurdles.
That includes local opposition to data centers ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and concerns from environmental groups.
Co-CEO Clay Magouyrk told analysts on the company's earnings call on Sept. 10 that Project Jupiter would not affect its previously stated fiscal 2027 revenue or earnings guidance.
Concerns have also mounted over Oracle's $18 billion in debt tied to the datacenter, which is already trading at stressed levels, according to the Financial Times.

articles.title_orig: As Xi meets Trump tomorrow, how do people in China view the U.S. now?
articles.title_zh: As Xi meets Trump tomorrow, how do people in China view the U.S. now?
articles.content_orig:
A red carpet and military flyover - How Trump welcomed Xi
US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.
His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view.
"China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.
You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.
For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax" .
China's foreign ministry warned that " narratives of threat " and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.
It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.
The US and China are locked in a race to develop AI
There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.
American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.
In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University , external .
Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.
OpenAI boss Sam Altman called for a coordinated slowdown of advanced AI development
The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.
So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success .
Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.
Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.
Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.
The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.
This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.
Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.
Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.
Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said.
"AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."
Yang Zhilin co-founded Moonshot, one of China's most successful AI models, in 2023
AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service.
"Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.
In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots , with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.
The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.
Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.
But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.
China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".
China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.
While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.
Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president.
"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".
Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.
China is the world's biggest manufacturer of robots
Beijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach.
Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control".
"China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said.
The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim.
Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all.
The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said.
"Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added.
Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap.
Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents.
While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
What we don't want, she added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI.

articles.title_orig: Track where a potent nor’easter will bring heavy rain, winds and waves
articles.title_zh: Track where a potent nor’easter will bring heavy rain, winds and waves
articles.content_orig:
Millions across the Northeast are bracing for an intense, multi-day Nor’easter this weekend that is forecast to bring heavy rain and strong wind gusts to the East Coast.
Forecast models still disagree on the storm’s exact track, but one thing is clear: wherever it goes, it will hit the region hard. Forecasters have high confidence in a long-duration onshore wind event that could bring significant coastal flooding.
Coastal flood warnings and high wind watches are already in place along much of the East Coast, with more alerts likely to be issued throughout the day Thursday.
The highest rainfall totals — 2 to 3 inches or more — are most likely from Rhode Island to eastern Massachusetts.
Powerful winds, including gusts up to 50-60 mph, risk toppling power lines and trees. Small shifts in the storm’s track will determine where outages and downed trees are most likely to occur.
Coastal flooding is expected to run 1 to 3 feet above high tide, and a full moon Saturday night could intensify the tides and worsen the flooding. Waves along the coast are expected to reach 12 feet in Ocean City, New Jersey, and up to 22 feet in New England.
Moderate to major flooding is likely from North Carolina to Nantucket, Massachusetts, with southeastern Virginia — particularly the Virginia Beach-to-Norfolk area — at highest risk for major coastal inundation of 1 to 3 feet.
Meanwhile, a separate storm is already pummeling the Eastern Seaboard, generating high winds and rough surf.
In Massachusetts, residents were seen this week hauling their boats out of the bay, worried about high tides and flooding from the Nor’easter. One person told NBC News he’d been “prepping all week for both wind and water.”
One couple even changed their wedding plans because of the storm — they had been set to marry this weekend on a Massachusetts beach.
And the Boston Red Sox moved Sunday’s game — the season finale — up to Friday to avoid any weather-related delays or cancellations.
In New Jersey, crews cleared debris from storm drains and flood-prone areas as emergency management officials urged residents to prepare for the incoming storm. Monmouth County Sheriff Shaun Golden recommended charging devices and stocking up on batteries ahead of possible power outages.
Elsewhere in the country, days of heavy rain in the Southwest have triggered major flooding, sending muddy waters sweeping through the streets of New Mexico. The El Paso, Texas, fire department said it has responded to more than 50 storm-related calls.
Off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, Tropical Storm Nolo threatens heavy rain and flash flooding, with more than 30 inches of rain  possible in some areas. Extreme rainfall remains the storm’s biggest risk.
Nolo currently has sustained winds of 50 mph and is expected to strengthen into a hurricane by Thursday night — potentially reaching Category 3 strength. As of the latest update, the storm was about 285 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, moving north at 2 mph.
Nolo is not expected to make direct landfall in Hawaii, but it could come close enough to bring tropical-storm-force winds to the Big Island and Maui as early as Thursday night, with hurricane-force winds possible by Friday night.
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Sam Brock is an NBC News correspondent.

Saudi Arabia will have assistance from a key Western ally in its fight against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis , as Britain is providing military support to the Kingdom in a bid to help restore stability in the region and ease pressures on the global energy supply.
“We’re working with our friends to try and deliver that de-escalation,” British Defense Minister Luke Pollard said in an interview Tuesday. The “purely defensive” deployment of an RAF Voyager to Saudi Arabia is intended to “ensure there’s no further escalation in the Red Sea, which could further risk our fuel prices,” he added.
The international assistance comes following weeks of fighting between the Saudi-backed government of Yemen and the Houthis, which shattered a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The Houthi rebels have made significant advances along the Red Sea coastline as they seek to tighten their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb , a critical maritime chokepoint that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. With global energy supplies already under strain due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war, the strangling of another trade route could further impact oil and fuel prices .
“Much of our trade, both in goods and in energy, comes through that part of the world. What happens in that part of the Middle East is absolutely vital for our own national security and our own economic security,” Pollard said, explaining why Britain responded to the Kingdom’s request for help.
When talking to reporters en route to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, ahead of his sit-down with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also cited the cost of living “pressures” at home as a key reason for the support and said he was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region.”
Burnham emphasized that it’s a “time-limited agreement in terms of the assistance that we will provide, but we will keep it under review.”
The support extended to Saudi Arabia marks Burnham’s first military deployment since he became Prime Minister in July. However, it’s far from the first time the U.K. has offered assistance to Saudi Arabia, as the two nations share a close military alliance.
The Ministry of Defense on Tuesday confirmed it had agreed to “provide an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi defensive activity” in the region. According to the British Royal Air Force (RAF), a Voyager provides strategic air support by allowing jets and other aircraft to refuel while in flight.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King's College London, says the Voyager “basically allows the Saudi Air Force to stay in the air over Yemen for longer without having to fly a single sortie and then returning to base.”
“It increases the operational tempo in terms of targeting strikes and being more flexible, and more agile in responding to changing situations on the ground,” he tells TIME.
According to Pollard, the Voyager is set to operate from the British RAF base in Cyprus, which was targeted by Iran earlier this year , and will support the British-built Typhoon jets used by Saudi Arabia. “That will help them with their defensive actions against the Houthis, who have been attacking not just the capital of Saudi Arabia in Riyadh, but also the Republic of Yemen as well,” he said.
Britain has historically held the role of “guarantor for maritime freedom of navigation all around the world,” says Krieg, describing the U.K.’s latest attempt to ease tensions over the Red Sea as an example of the government “stepping up to the plate.”
“We're not just helping a partner in the region,” he adds. “We're also helping ourselves, because the Houthis having the Bab al-Mandeb is not something that the U.K. can tolerate.”
Krieg says the move signifies a small success for Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states as they seek to strengthen bilateral security relationships beyond their traditional reliance on the U.S. This is “the worst security situation the Saudis have been in [for] a very long time,” he notes.
“Gulf states are trying to supplement the existing U.S. capabilities with all kinds of [other] agreements, like the Mecca pact ,” he says, referencing a trilateral defense security pact made between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August. “The U.K. wants to be seen as being active and being there when a friend is in need.”
The U.K. and Saudi Arabia share an alliance that dates back to almost a century ago.
“It's a very long, strategic partnership,” says Krieg. “It goes back to the early days of the current Kingdom, where Britain, at the time, was still the only superpower in the world, and was controlling the waterways and a lot of the territories in Arabia, including in South Yemen.”
Britain was among the first governments to recognize the independent territories of Saudi Arabia through the Treaty of Jeddah in 1927, which helped solidify the boundaries of the nascent kingdom ahead of the formation of modern Saudi Arabia in 1932.
Decades later, the U.K. supported the Saudi-led military coalition in its campaign against the Houthis from 2015 until the 2022 truce.
According to the Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT), the published value of U.K. arms export licenses to Saudi Arabia from the start of the bombing campaign in March 2015 through the April 2022 truce was £7.1 billion ($9.4 billion).
“The two main Western backers of the Saudi Kingdom are the Americans and the British,” says David Wearing, an assistant professor in international relations at the University of Sussex. “From the British and the American point of view, the Middle East is strategically important because it's a huge source of global energy suppliers, oil, and gas.”
In late 2023, the Houthis started disrupted shipping in the Red Sea, targeting cargo ships they said were linked to Israel, in what they described as a show of support for Palestinians in Gaza . Amid concerns over the impact on the world economy, the U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024, striking multiple Houthi targets in Yemen. In April 2025, the U.K. government participated in another joint operation with the U.S. against a Houthi military facility in Yemen.
In March of this year, the U.K. deployed a Sky Sabre , the army’s medium range air defense missile system, to Saudi Arabia to defend the Kingdom against Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The U.K. government's Strategic Export Controls Annual Report of 2025 described the military relationship with Saudi Arabia as a “longstanding” partnership providing “Typhoon, Tornado, and Hawk aircraft, mine countermeasure vessels, and associated munitions, infrastructure, logistics and manpower support packages.”
BAE Systems—a major British defense, aerospace, and security company—said in its own 2025 report that Saudi Arabia was its largest customer by sales in its air business.
Saudi Arabia has reportedly sought assistance from allies to stave off Houthi advances. France , Pakistan , and Egypt issued strong statements condemning the Houthi attacks, but have not publicly announced new military support for the Kingdom.
